title: The Weight of Invisible Work: What Shipping a VS Code Extension Taught Me About Developer Tooling
excerpt: Building tools for developers means solving problems they didn't know they had—and that requires listening more than coding.

content.text: When I started building CodeLoom Explorer, I thought the hardest part would be parsing Dart ASTs or rendering React Flow graphs. I was wrong. The hardest part was watching someone use my extension for the first time and realizing they immediately closed it because it didn't solve a problem they actually cared about.
Tools Are Only as Good as the Pain They Remove

I spent weeks perfecting the graph visualization in CodeLoom Explorer. Node clustering, color-coded dependencies, smooth zoom animations. Then I watched a colleague open it, glance at the screen for three seconds, and go back to their terminal. The tool worked exactly as designed—and failed completely.

That moment taught me something fundamental about developer tooling: functionality is not value. A tool only matters if it removes friction from a workflow that already exists. Before writing a single line of code, I should have asked: what task are developers repeating daily that they hate doing?
Build tools for problems people have, not problems you think they should have.
content.author: Roshan Lal Yogi

content.text: The Invisible Work of Understanding Context

After that failed demo, I changed my approach. Instead of jumping straight into implementation, I started spending time in developer Discord servers, reading GitHub issues, and watching screen recordings of people coding. I noticed something interesting: developers don't struggle with understanding their own code—they struggle with understanding code they haven't touched in months.

CodeLoom Explorer evolved from a generic dependency visualizer into a tool that surfaces context around code changes. When you open a file, it shows you the last person who modified each function, related files that might break, and a mini knowledge graph of how this piece fits into the larger system. It's less flashy than animated graphs, but it solves a real problem.
Privacy-First Isn't Just a Marketing Term

Making CodeLoom Explorer privacy-first wasn't just about ethics—it was about trust. Developers are rightfully paranoid about tools that read their codebase. Every network request, every data collection point becomes a potential security concern.

We process everything locally using the VS Code extension API. No code ever leaves the developer's machine. The extension uses the Language Server Protocol to analyze code in-memory, and all graph data is stored in a local IndexedDB instance. This constraint forced us to optimize aggressively, which ironically made the tool faster than many cloud-based alternatives.

Here's what I learned about developers: they want tools that are infinitely customizable, but they also want to spend zero time configuring them. They complain about bloated IDEs, but they install dozens of extensions. They want everything integrated, but they don't want to learn new workflows.

With CodeLoom Explorer, we embraced this paradox by shipping with sensible defaults that work out of the box, while exposing configuration options for power users. The graph visualization appears automatically when you open a project, but you can customize node colors, clustering algorithms, and information density through a simple settings panel.

I almost didn't ship CodeLoom Explorer because it wasn't perfect. The graph rendering was slow on large codebases, some edge cases in the AST parsing weren't handled, and the UI felt clunky compared to my mental mockups.

Then I remembered why I started building tools in the first place: to make my own development experience better. I published a rough version to the VS Code marketplace, and within a week, a user submitted a pull request that fixed the performance issue I'd been struggling with for months. Another user suggested a feature that completely changed how we thought about the tool.

The extension now has over 10,000 active users. Not because it's perfect, but because it solves a real problem that real developers face every day. And that's the difference between building something interesting and building something useful.
These days, whenever I start a new project—whether it's Bolo AI, SyncMind, or something entirely new—I ask myself one question before writing any code: what invisible work am I about to make visible?
